questions.problem: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=3-{x}^{2}$ and $y=x+1,$ then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14158460/assets/7316d667d7308ac5ec0f5348055d3d0e7eb90b97abaa74f5693c3151dc3b8bb1.png)

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{x}^{2} & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14158460/assets/aab6fb99694b518bfa9d200a75876c9e888ba1ab7d699464bc9caca360be775a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 1,\,x+1\le y\le 3-{x}^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}[{\int }_{x+1}^{3-{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\text{ }dy]dx\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡x\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}3x{e}^{y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{e}^{y}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}-{e}^{0})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3x(x-1)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(3{x}^{2}-3x)dx & ={[{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(64-24)-(1-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =40+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,2{x}^{2}\le y\le {x}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{2{x}^{2}}^{{x}^{2}+1}dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})dx & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}x & =5-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x-5 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-x-10 & =0 \\ (x+2)(2x-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We discard the solution $x=\frac{5}{2}$ since $x\le 0$ in our region. Therefore, $x$-limits are $-2\le x\le 0.$

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 0,\,-\frac{1}{2}x\le y\le 5-{x}^{2}\}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-x/2}^{5-{x}^{2}}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-2) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
